newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - Iraq says oil embargo hurting West.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Iraq says oil embargo hurting West.

text.p: In a warning to the West that the world oil supply is vulnerable, Iraq's chief oil negotiator said on Thursday that the embargo on Iraqi oil was "dangerous" given rising crude prices and limited spare production capacity.
Ambassador Abdul Amir al-Anbari also said the continued "unilateral disarmament" of Iraq could invite aggression and upset the balance of power in the Middle East region.
As head of an Iraqi delegation, he was addressing a two-day seminar in Geneva on the impact of international sanctions, sponsored by the Swiss-based Crans-Montana forum.
Earlier, in an interview with Reuters, al-Anbari said that he did not expect any change in the U.S. position on the stalled oil-for-food deal until January 1997 at the earliest.
He blamed Washington for the delay in implementing the humanitarian pact signed last May with the United Nations.
Under the plan, Iraq would be allowed to export $2 billion of oil over renewable six-month periods to buy sorely-needed food and medicine to ease the effects of sweeping sanctions.
Iraq, once a major oil exporter, remains under economic sanctions imposed since its August 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

OPEC and other oil producers have enjoyed windfall revenues this year as Middle East tensions, strong demand and very low heating oil stocks ahead of the peak winter fuel use period have pushed prices to their highest levels in nearly six years.

"As long as the oil embargo is in force, price fluctuation is bound to continue mainly upward in vain for lack of any spare capacity outside OPEC and the limited production spare capacity within OPEC, mainly in Saudi Arabia, which is estimated to be less than three million barrels per day...representing less than four per cent of global consumption of oil," al-Anbari said in a speech. "The present world oil supply is vulnerable.
"It is in this context that the dangerous impact of the embargo on Iraqi oil is greatest. It is a very dangerous and very thin margin."
"Any interruption of oil supplies because of any crisis in the world would lead prices far higher, causing panic and sending the world global economy into great recession."

The price of the official crude "basket" of the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), the average of prices of seven different crude grades, has been above OPEC's own target of $21 a barrel for months.

Al-Anbari dismissed as a "cover-up" allegations by U.S. envoy Madeleine Albright that President Saddam Hussein was deliberately holding up the oil deal by making what she called "outrageous demands" on U.N. staff assigned to monitor it.
"Iraq had presented a pricing formula and is ready to go ahead with oil sale once the pricing formula is approved by the United States," he told Reuters in an interview.

Asked when he expected the deal to be implemented, he replied: "Actually, it is up to the United States because only the United States has refused to approve the pricing formula presented by Iraq to the Sanctions Committee.
"They don't even say why they don't approve it."
Al-Anbari, asked whether he expected any breakthrough in implementing the pact before an OPEC ministerial meeting on November 27, replied: "I hope so, but frankly I doubt it.

"I believe the U.S. is holding their position until January 1997. They have not indicated this, but this is how I read their position from past experience," added al-Anbari, who struck the oil-for-food deal in 50 negotiating sessions with the United Nations between February and May.

Al-Anbari said the United States was alone in rejecting the pricing formula proposed by Baghdad which would be used in oil sales contracts. But Albright last week dismissed the oil-pricing controversy as a "phony issue" raised by Iraq.
